Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly, meaning you might have mild symptoms or none at all for years.
Common Early Warning Signs
Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to clear extra glucose, which pulls water from your tissues and makes you run to the bathroom more often—especially at night.
Constant fatigue: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly for energy, leaving you feeling exhausted even after a full night's rest.
Increased hunger: You may feel very hungry shortly after eating because your body fails to convert food into usable cellular energy.
Blurred vision: Extra sugar in the bloodstream changes fluid levels and temporarily alters the shape of the lenses in your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: High blood sugar impairs blood flow and nerve function, making minor bruises, scrapes, or cuts take much longer to heal.
Frequent infections: Bacteria and yeast thrive on excess sugar, leading to frequent urinary tract infections (UTIs) or yeast infections.
Tingling or numbness: Mild pain, numbness, or a "pins and needles" sensation in the hands or feet can signal early nerve irritation.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark skin patches (called acanthosis nigricans) around the armpits, neck, or groin often point to underlying insulin resistance.
What to Do Next
If you notice these signs, check resources from the American Diabetes Association or visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to learn more. A doctor can confirm a diagnosis using simple blood tests like a fasting glucose or A1C test.

Which specific symptoms you or someone else is experiencing
How long these signs have been present
I can help you prepare questions to discuss with a healthcare provider.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood tests that measure the amount of sugar (glucose) in your blood.
Doctors rely on four main diagnostic tests:
Common Diagnostic Tests
A1C Test: This test measures your average blood sugar level over the past two to three months. A result of 6.5% or higher means you have diabetes. No fasting is required.
Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) Test: This test measures your blood sugar after you do not eat or drink anything except water for at least eight hours. A result of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher indicates diabetes.
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT): This test checks your blood sugar before and two hours after you drink a special sugary liquid. A reading of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher at the two-hour mark confirms diabetes.
Random Plasma Glucose Test: This test checks your blood sugar at any time of day if you show severe symptoms like extreme thirst or frequent urination. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher suggests diabetes.
Confirmation and Screening
Confirmation: If you do not have clear symptoms, doctors usually repeat the abnormal test on a different day to confirm the diagnosis.
You can read more about these diagnostic thresholds on the American Diabetes Association.
For detailed guidance on condition management, visit Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic.
If you'd like, tell me:
What symptoms (if any) you or someone else are experiencing
Any risk factors like family history or age
I can provide more tailored information.

Treatment for type 2 diabetes involves lifestyle changes, blood sugar monitoring, and medications or insulin to keep glucose levels in a healthy range.
Lifestyle Interventions
Diet changes: Focus on high-fiber foods, non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, and complex carbohydrates while limiting processed foods and added sugars.
Physical activity: Get at least 150 minutes of regular exercise weekly to help lower blood sugar and improve insulin sensitivity.
Weight management: Reach and maintain a healthy weight to reduce the severity of insulin resistance.
Medications
Metformin: Metformin is typically the first oral medication prescribed; it reduces glucose production in the liver and improves insulin sensitivity.
GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP agonists: Injectable medications (such as Ozemic or Victoza) that stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and often assist with weight loss.
SGLT2 inhibitors: Oral drugs that help the body remove extra glucose through urine.
Sulfonylureas: Oral medications that prompt the pancreas to make more insulin.
DPP-4 inhibitors: Oral pills that help lower blood glucose by keeping helpful digestive chemicals active longer.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Medications that improve insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat cells.
Insulin and Advanced Options
Insulin therapy: Synthetic insulin given via injections, pens, or a pump if oral medications and lifestyle steps do not control blood sugar adequately.
Bariatric surgery: Weight-loss surgery that can significantly improve or remit type 2 diabetes in certain individuals.

Are you looking for information on a newly diagnosed case or adjusting an existing treatment plan?
Do you have specific concerns about side effects or injectable versus oral options?

Jardiance (empagliflozin) commonly causes increased urination, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and genital yeast infections.
Common Side Effects
Urinating more often: Extra sugar leaves your body through your urine, which pulls more water with it. Taking your dose in the morning can help prevent overnight bathroom trips.
UTIs: Higher sugar levels in urine allow bacteria to grow more easily, causing burning, pain, or urgency when you pee.
Genital yeast infections: These affect both women (vaginal yeast infections) and men (skin infections around the penis), causing itching, redness, or discharge.
Increased thirst and mild dehydration: Fluid loss can lead to dry mouth or mild dizziness when standing up.
Other mild effects: Upper respiratory tract infections (like a common cold), joint pain, or mild nausea.
Rare and Serious Side Effects
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood—even with normal blood sugar levels—marked by nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, trouble breathing, and fruity-smelling breath.
Dehydration and kidney injury: Severe fluid loss that can cause dizziness, fainting, or sudden worsening of kidney function.
Fournier’s Gangrene: A rare but severe and life-threatening genital or perineal bacterial infection causing intense pain, swelling, redness, and fever.
Severe allergic reactions: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or trouble breathing.
Low blood sugar (Hypoglycemia): More likely if combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.
You can review full safety guidelines and prescribing details directly on the Jardiance Official Site. You can also read more about managing reactions through GoodRx on Jardiance Side Effects.
If you are taking Jardiance, let me know:
Are you experiencing any specific symptoms right now?
Are you combining it with insulin or other diabetes medications?
I can help you understand when to contact your doctor.

While metformin remains the traditional first choice for type 2 diabetes, modern guidelines recommend choosing between SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists as early treatment based on your specific heart, kidney, and weight goals .
SGLT2 Inhibitors
What they are: Oral pills taken once daily. Examples include empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin.
How they work: They help your kidneys remove extra sugar through your urine.
Best for: Patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease, as they protect heart and kidney function and slow organ damage.
Side effects: Higher risk of genital and urinary tract infections.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
What they are: Injectable medications (given weekly or daily), though oral options are also available. Examples include semaglutide (Ozempic).
How they work: They trigger insulin release, stop your liver from making too much sugar, and slow down digestion so you feel full.
Best for: Patients who need significant weight loss or have a high risk of heart attacks and strokes (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease).
Side effects: Stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
How to Choose
Choose SGLT2 inhibitors if you have kidney disease or heart failure.
Choose GLP-1 receptor agonists if weight loss and strong blood sugar control are your top priorities.
You can check to compare copay savings and prescription costs, as both drug classes can be expensive.
To help narrow down which option fits you best, tell me:
Do you have any heart or kidney conditions ?
Is weight loss a major goal for you?
Do you prefer a daily pill or an injectable medication ?

High blood pressure (hypertension) usually has no signs or symptoms at all, which is why it is called the "silent killer".
Common Misconceptions
Most people feel completely normal even when their numbers are very high.
Headaches, nosebleeds, or facial flushing do not reliably mean your blood pressure is high, except during a severe spike.
Signs of a Hypertensive Emergency
When blood pressure rises to dangerous levels (usually above 180/120 mm Hg), it can cause critical damage. Call 911 immediately if you have extremely high readings along with any of these warning signs:
Chest pain or pressure
Shortness of breath
Sudden vision changes
Difficulty speaking or confusion
Numbness or weakness on one side of the body
Severe, sudden headache
How to Know Your Status
The only way to find out if you have high blood pressure is to measure it using a cuff.
You can get checked at an annual doctor visit, at a local pharmacy, or with a home monitor.
Learn more about guidelines and risks from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or the American Heart Association.
If you want, tell me:
What was your last blood pressure reading?
Are you experiencing any current symptoms?
I can help you understand what those numbers mean or when to seek care.

High blood pressure (hypertension) is defined as a reading of 130/80 mm Hg or higher.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and major health organizations, blood pressure readings are grouped into distinct categories:
Blood Pressure Categories
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: Systolic between 120–129 and diastolic less than 80
Stage 1 Hypertension: Systolic 130–139 OR diastolic 80–89 mm Hg
Stage 2 Hypertension: Systolic 140 or higher OR diastolic 90 or higher mm Hg
Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 systolic and/or higher than 120 diastolic (requires immediate medical care)
Note: The top number is systolic (pressure when the heart beats) and the bottom number is diastolic (pressure when the heart rests between beats).

Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) include healthy daily habits and prescription medicines.
Lifestyle Changes
Lose weight: Shedding extra pounds lightens the workload on your heart.
Eat healthy food: Choose a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while cutting back on salt.
Exercise often: Try to do regular aerobic activity, like brisk walking, most days of the week.
Limit alcohol: Drink in moderation or avoid alcohol completely.
Quit smoking: Stopping smoking helps protect your blood vessels and overall heart health.
Common Medications
Doctors often start with one of four main drug classes, which you can read more about via the Cleveland Clinic Antihypertensives Guide:
ACE inhibitors: These relax your blood vessels by stopping the body from making a hormone that narrows them (examples include lisinopril and ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II receptor blockers): These block that same hormone from tightening your blood vessels (examples include losartan and valsartan). They work similarly to ACE inhibitors but do not cause a dry cough.
Calcium channel blockers: These keep calcium out of the muscle cells in your heart and blood vessels so the vessels can relax and widen (examples include amlodipine and diltiazem).
Diuretics (water pills): These help your kidneys flush extra salt and water from your body, lowering fluid in the blood (examples include hydrochlorothiazide).
If one medicine is not enough, doctors often combine two or more low-dose pills from different classes to reach a healthy blood pressure goal.
If you'd like, please share:
Your recent blood pressure readings if you know them
Any other health conditions you have (like diabetes or kidney disease)
I can give you more tailored details on what doctors usually recommend for those specific situations.

Common side effects of losartan include dizziness, fatigue, upper respiratory infections, and mild stomach upset.
You can review comprehensive data on Losartan via MedlinePlus or check the detailed NHS Losartan Guide for more patient information. Additional clinical descriptions are maintained by the Mayo Clinic Drug Directory.
Common Side Effects
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Happens when your blood pressure drops, especially when standing up quickly.
Fatigue: Feeling more tired than usual as your body adapts to lower blood pressure.
Upper respiratory symptoms: Stuffiness, nasal congestion, or signs of a common cold.
Digestive issues: Mild nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach pain.
Aches and pains: Back pain or occasional joint pain.
Headache: Mild head pain during the initial adjustment phase.
Serious Side Effects
High potassium levels (Hyperkalemia): May cause muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat, though it often has no symptoms.
Low blood pressure (Hypotension): Can lead to fainting, confusion, or blurred vision.
Kidney function changes: May show up as decreased urination or swelling in the hands, ankles, or feet.
Allergic reaction (Angioedema): Rare swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, which makes breathing or swallowing difficult.
If you are experiencing specific symptoms, please let me know:
What symptoms are you or the person taking losartan experiencing?
How long have you been taking the medication?
I can provide more tailored guidance or help you determine when to contact a doctor.

ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are equally recommended as first-line medications for high blood pressure, but ARBs offer a safer side-effect profile.
Effectiveness in Lowering Blood Pressure
Equal blood pressure control: Both drug classes lower blood pressure effectively by relaxing your blood vessels.
Similar heart and kidney protection: Large studies show no significant difference between ACE inhibitors and ARBs in preventing heart attacks, strokes, or overall heart events.
Equal guideline status: Major health organizations rank both classes as top-tier choices for initial therapy, detailed further in the American Heart Association Study .
Side Effects and Tolerability
Dry cough: ACE inhibitors often cause an annoying, dry cough because they change a chemical in the body called bradykinin. ARBs do not affect bradykinin and rarely cause a cough.
Angioedema: ACE inhibitors carry a higher risk of angioedema, which is a dangerous swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat. ARBs have a much lower risk of this reaction.
Patient drop-out rates: Because ARBs cause fewer bothersome side effects, patients are slightly less likely to stop taking them compared to ACE inhibitors, as supported by the Cochrane Systematic Review.
Important Safety Rules
No pregnancy: Neither ACE inhibitors nor ARBs should be used during pregnancy because they can harm an unborn baby.
Never combine them: You should never take an ACE inhibitor and an ARB at the same time, as the combination increases risks like high potassium and kidney damage without adding extra heart benefits.
If you are deciding between these medications, please tell me:
Are you currently taking one of these drugs and experiencing a dry cough ?
Do you have other conditions like diabetes or kidney disease?
I can help you prepare questions to discuss with your doctor.

The most common symptom of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is shortness of breath that starts during physical activity and eventually happens at rest.
PAH is high blood pressure in the arteries of your lungs. In the early stages, you might not notice any signs at all. As the condition progresses and puts strain on the heart, symptoms become more noticeable.
Common Symptoms
Shortness of breath during daily tasks like climbing stairs or exercising.
Fatigue and a general lack of energy.
Swelling (edema) in the feet, ankles, legs, and later the belly or neck due to fluid build-up.
Dizziness or fainting spells, especially during physical exertion.
Chest pain or pressure.
Heart palpitations or a racing, pounding heartbeat.
Bluish lips or fingers (cyanosis) caused by lower oxygen levels.
You can learn more about these signs through the American Lung Association.

The most common side effects of Opsumit (macitentan) include a stuffy or runny nose, sore throat, bronchitis, headache, flu-like symptoms, and urinary tract infections.
Serious Side Effects
Serious birth defects: Opsumit can harm an unborn baby and must not be taken during pregnancy.
Liver problems: It can cause liver damage. Watch for nausea, vomiting, upper right stomach pain, extreme tiredness, loss of appetite, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin/eyes (jaundice).
Fluid retention: Swelling in the hands, legs, ankles, or feet, or rapid weight gain can happen, usually within the first few weeks.
Low red blood cells (Anemia): This can cause unusual tiredness, weakness, or pale skin.
Decreased sperm counts: Opsumit may affect male fertility.
You can check out more details on the Opsumit Safety Information page.

Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are equally recommended as top-tier, first-line medications for high blood pressure .
How They Work
ACE inhibitors (names ending in "-pril", like lisinopril) stop your body from making a hormone called angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels.
(names ending in "-sartan", like losartan) block the receptor sites where angiotensin II attaches, keeping blood vessels relaxed.
Both lower blood pressure effectively and protect the heart and kidneys.
Key Differences
Side Effects: ARBs are safer and better tolerated. ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent dry cough and carry a higher risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips or tongue) because they increase bradykinin levels. ARBs do not affect bradykinin, avoiding the dry cough.
Effectiveness: Large studies show both classes lower blood pressure and reduce heart attack or stroke risk equally well.
Cost: ACE inhibitors are usually generic and less expensive than ARBs.
Clinical Preference
Recent large-scale data and guidelines increasingly favor prescribing ARBs over ACE inhibitors initially because patients are much less likely to stop taking ARBs due to side effects. Neither class should be used during pregnancy.

Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) include healthy daily habits and prescription medicines.
Lifestyle Changes
Lose weight: Shedding extra pounds lightens the workload on your heart.
Eat healthy food: Choose a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while cutting back on salt.
Exercise often: Try to do regular aerobic activity, like brisk walking, most days of the week.
Limit alcohol: Drink in moderation or avoid alcohol completely.
Quit smoking: Stopping smoking helps protect your blood vessels and overall heart health.
Common Medications
Doctors often start with one of four main drug classes, which you can read more about via the Cleveland Clinic Antihypertensives Guide:
ACE inhibitors: These relax your blood vessels by stopping the body from making a hormone that narrows them (examples include lisinopril and ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II receptor blockers): These block that same hormone from tightening your blood vessels (examples include losartan and valsartan). They work similarly to ACE inhibitors but do not cause a dry cough.
Calcium channel blockers: These keep calcium out of the muscle cells in your heart and blood vessels so the vessels can relax and widen (examples include amlodipine and diltiazem).
Diuretics (water pills): These help your kidneys flush extra salt and water from your body, lowering fluid in the blood (examples include hydrochlorothiazide).
If one medicine is not enough, doctors often combine two or more low-dose pills from different classes to reach a healthy blood pressure goal.

ACE inhibitors and ARBs (Angiotensin Receptor Blockers) work equally well to lower blood pressure, but have a better safety and tolerability profile.
Effectiveness
Blood pressure control: Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce blood pressure equally by inhibiting the renin-angiotensin system.
Cardiovascular outcomes: Large studies show no significant difference between the two classes regarding heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, or cardiovascular death.
Safety and Side Effects
Dry cough: ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent dry cough (due to a buildup of bradykinin), whereas ARBs do not.
Angioedema: Serious swelling of the face or throat is rare, but significantly more common with ACE inhibitors than ARBs.
Discontinuation: Patients are less likely to stop treatment on an ARB due to side effects.
Shared risks: Both classes carry a risk of high potassium levels (hyperkalemia) and low blood pressure (hypotension), and both are strictly contraindicated during pregnancy.
Clinical Recommendation
Current guidelines from major cardiology groups list both ACE inhibitors and ARBs as top-tier, first-line options for hypertension.
However, modern large-scale comparative data suggest that ARBs should be preferentially prescribed over ACE inhibitors as an initial choice because they provide identical blood pressure control with fewer adverse events.
Patients already doing well and tolerating an ACE inhibitor do not routinely need to switch.

Early signs of type 2 diabetes often develop slowly, meaning you might have mild symptoms or none at all for years.

Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work overtime to clear extra glucose, which pulls water from your tissues and makes you run to the bathroom more often—especially at night.
Constant fatigue: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly for energy, leaving you feeling exhausted even after a full night's rest.
Increased hunger: You may feel very hungry shortly after eating because your body fails to convert food into usable cellular energy.
Blurred vision: Extra sugar in the bloodstream changes fluid levels and temporarily alters the shape of the lenses in your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: High blood sugar impairs blood flow and nerve function, making minor bruises, scrapes, or cuts take much longer to heal.

Tingling or numbness: Mild pain, numbness, or a "pins and needles" sensation in the hands or feet can signal early nerve irritation.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark skin patches (called acanthosis nigricans) around the armpits, neck, or groin often point to underlying insulin resistance.
What to Do Next
If you notice these signs, check resources from the American Diabetes Association or visit the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to learn more. A doctor can confirm a diagnosis using simple blood tests like a fasting glucose or A1C test.

Common side effects of Jardiance include increased urination, urinary tract infections (UTIs), and genital yeast infections.
Common and Mild Side Effects
Increased urination: Passing more urine or needing to go more often happens because the medication removes extra sugar through your kidneys.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs): Extra sugar in the urine can help bacteria grow, causing burning or pain when you pee.
Genital yeast infections: These can affect both women and men, causing itching, discomfort, or redness.
Upper respiratory tract infections: Mild cold-like symptoms, such as a stuffy nose or sore throat.
Increased thirst and mild dehydration: Losing extra fluid can make you feel thirsty or slightly dizzy.
Rare and Serious Side Effects
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): A dangerous buildup of acid in the blood, marked by nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, and trouble breathing.
Severe dehydration and low blood pressure: Can cause dizziness, fainting, or sudden worsening of kidney function.
Necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier’s gangrene): A rare, serious, and painful tissue infection in the genital and anal area.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): More likely if you take Jardiance along with insulin or other diabetes medications.
Lower limb amputations: A rare risk involving new pain, sores, or infections in the legs or feet.
Serious allergic reactions: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or trouble breathing.

Metformin remains the standard first-line medication for type 2 diabetes, but SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly prioritized early or alongside metformin based on individual organ protection goals.
Core Differences
SGLT2 Inhibitors (e.g., ): Oral pills taken once daily. They excel at protecting the kidneys and managing or preventing heart failure. They lower A1C by about 0.5% to 1% and cause modest weight loss. Common side effects include genital and urinary tract infections.
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (e.g., Ozempic): Mostly weekly injections, though some oral options exist. They excel at lowering blood sugar (reducing A1C by up to 1.5% to 2%) and promoting substantial weight loss. They also lower the risk of major cardiovascular events like stroke. Common side effects are gastrointestinal, such as nausea and vomiting.
Choosing Based on Comorbidities
Clinical guidelines from groups like the American Diabetes Association recommend choosing between the two classes depending on specific health conditions:
Choose an SGLT2 inhibitor first if: You have a history of heart failure or chronic kidney disease.
Choose a GLP-1 receptor agonist first if: Your primary goals are significant weight loss, reducing obesity-related cardiometabolic risk, or lowering atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk (like stroke prevention).

High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called a "silent killer" because it typically causes no signs or symptoms at all.
The Silent Nature of Hypertension
No warning signs: Most people with high blood pressure feel completely normal and do not realize their pressure is high.
The only way to know: Measuring your blood pressure with a cuff monitor is the only reliable way to detect the condition.
Symptoms of a Hypertensive Crisis (Emergency)
When blood pressure spikes to dangerously high levels (above 180/120 mm Hg), it can cause a medical emergency. Call 911 immediately if you have a reading over 180/120 combined with any of these critical symptoms:
Chest pain or tightness
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Sudden, severe headache
Numbness or sudden weakness
Changes in vision
Difficulty speaking or confusion
Sudden, severe back or abdominal pain
Subtle Signs of Elevated Pressure
While not reliable early warnings, some individuals experiencing severely elevated blood pressure or rapid spikes may notice:
Early-morning headaches
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Blurry vision
Nosebleeds
Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)

Blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or higher is generally considered high blood pressure (hypertension).
Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers:
Systolic (top number): Pressure when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): Pressure when your heart rests between beats.
Blood Pressure Categories
According to the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the stages are:
Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg
Elevated: 120–129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic
Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 systolic and/or higher than 120 diastolic (requires immediate medical attention)

Treatment options for hypertension (high blood pressure) include healthy daily habits and prescription medicines.
Lifestyle Changes
Lose weight: Shedding extra pounds lightens the workload on your heart.
Eat healthy food: Choose a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while cutting back on salt.
Exercise often: Try to do regular aerobic activity, like brisk walking, most days of the week.
Limit alcohol: Drink in moderation or avoid alcohol completely.
Quit smoking: Stopping smoking helps protect your blood vessels and overall heart health.
Common Medications
Doctors often start with one of four main drug classes, which you can read more about via the Cleveland Clinic Antihypertensives Guide:
ACE inhibitors: These relax your blood vessels by stopping the body from making a hormone that narrows them (examples include lisinopril and ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II receptor blockers): These block that same hormone from tightening your blood vessels (examples include losartan and valsartan). They work similarly to ACE inhibitors but do not cause a dry cough.
Calcium channel blockers: These keep calcium out of the muscle cells in your heart and blood vessels so the vessels can relax and widen (examples include amlodipine and diltiazem).
Diuretics (water pills): These help your kidneys flush extra salt and water from your body, lowering fluid in the blood (examples include hydrochlorothiazide).
If one medicine is not enough, doctors often combine two or more low-dose pills from different classes to reach a healthy blood pressure goal.

Losartan commonly causes mild side effects like dizziness, tiredness, and stuffy nose, but can rarely lead to serious issues like high potassium or kidney changes.
Common Side Effects
Dizziness or lightheadedness: Happens when blood pressure drops, especially upon standing.
Fatigue: Feeling more tired as your body adjusts to lower blood pressure.
Cold symptoms: Stuffy nose, sneezing, or mild sore throat.
Digestive upset: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or mild stomach pain.
Back or joint pain: Aching muscles or stiffness in the joints.
Headache: Mild head pain during the first few weeks.
Serious Side Effects
High potassium (hyperkalemia): Can cause muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat.
Kidney problems: May lead to swelling in the legs or a big change in urination.
Low blood pressure (hypotension): Causes severe dizziness, confusion, or fainting.
Severe allergic reaction (angioedema): Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, making it hard to breathe.
Pregnancy warning: Losartan can cause severe harm or death to an unborn baby and must be stopped immediately if you become pregnant.

ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are both recommended as equal first-line options to treat high blood pressure, but generally have a safer and better-tolerated side effect profile.
How They Work
ACE inhibitors (names ending in "-pril," like lisinopril) stop the body from making high levels of angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels.
(names ending in "-sartan," like losartan) block the receptor sites where angiotensin II attaches, which relaxes blood vessels.
Both lower blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels and reducing strain on the heart.
Effectiveness and Safety
Effectiveness: Large studies show that both drug classes lower blood pressure and protect the heart and kidneys equally well.
Side Effects: ACE inhibitors frequently cause a persistent dry cough and carry a small risk of (severe swelling of the tissue under the skin) because they affect a chemical called bradykinin. ARBs do not affect bradykinin, meaning they do not cause the dry cough and have a much lower risk of angioedema.
Cost: ACE inhibitors are often generic and less expensive, whereas ARBs can cost slightly more.

The most common symptom of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is shortness of breath that starts during physical activity and eventually happens at rest.
PAH is high blood pressure in the arteries of your lungs. In the early stages, you might not notice any signs at all. As the condition progresses and puts strain on the heart, symptoms become more noticeable.
Common Symptoms
Shortness of breath during daily tasks like climbing stairs or exercising.
Fatigue and a general lack of energy.
Swelling (edema) in the feet, ankles, legs, and later the belly or neck due to fluid build-up.
Dizziness or fainting spells, especially during physical exertion.
Chest pain or pressure.
Heart palpitations or a racing, pounding heartbeat.
Bluish lips or fingers (cyanosis) caused by lower oxygen levels.
You can learn more about these signs through the American Lung Association.

The most common side effects of Opsumit (macitentan) include a stuffy or runny nose, sore throat, bronchitis, headache, flu-like symptoms, and urinary tract infections.
Serious Side Effects
Serious birth defects: Opsumit can harm an unborn baby and must not be taken during pregnancy.
Liver problems: It can cause liver damage. Watch for nausea, vomiting, upper right stomach pain, extreme tiredness, loss of appetite, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin/eyes (jaundice).
Fluid retention: Swelling in the hands, legs, ankles, or feet, or rapid weight gain can happen, usually within the first few weeks.
Low red blood cells (Anemia): This can cause unusual tiredness, weakness, or pale skin.
Decreased sperm counts: Opsumit may affect male fertility.
You can check out more details on the Opsumit Safety Information page.
